---
title: "Stable Capability Fields and Governed Replacement"
unit_id: "unit-09"

## The Name That Survives the Upgrade

Imagine that the repository from Part I has acquired a patch verifier. Before a
change can merge, the verifier reads the proposed diff, checks the affected
interfaces, runs selected tests, looks for policy violations, and returns one
of three results: accept, reject, or ask for human review. Other tools now call
it by a stable name. Maintainers write procedures around it. Approval rules
refer to it. Audit logs say that the patch verifier approved a release.

Then a better verifier appears.

It is faster on ordinary patches and catches several defects the old one
missed. It uses a newer model, a different prompt, another retrieval index, and
a more aggressive test selector. On a benchmark it wins decisively. Replacing
the old verifier looks like an obvious upgrade.

But what, exactly, is being replaced? The command name can stay the same while
the meaning changes underneath it. The new verifier may abstain less often,
interpret policy language differently, omit an audit field, tolerate a class
of flaky tests, read more of the repository, send context to a remote service,
or take actions that the old verifier could only recommend. Its average score
may rise while a rare security regression returns. Its output schema may be
compatible while its authority expands. A clean software deployment can
therefore move the terms of trust without changing the name that everyone
relies on.

This is a general problem for an improving AI system. Models, tools, prompts,
policies, memories, evaluators, data, hardware, and organizations will all
change. A system that cannot replace them becomes brittle. A system that
replaces them by reputation, benchmark rank, or mutable registry flag becomes
unaccountable. Improvement requires continuity, but continuity cannot mean
freezing the implementation forever.

The proposed answer has two parts. First, give the capability a stable field:
a versioned statement of what the capability means for a particular consumer,
use, environment, threat model, and period of evidence. Second, treat every
replacement as a governed transaction against that field. The field holds the
promise. The implementation is one defeasible attempt to keep it.

The phrase *stable capability field* can sound more mysterious than it is. The
idea is familiar whenever a durable role outlives its current occupant. A bank
account is not identical to the database process serving it. A public office is
not identical to one officeholder. A network service is not identical to one
binary. Stability belongs to the governed interface and its obligations, not
to the machinery currently realizing them.

The difficulty is that an AI capability has a richer contract than a function
signature. The patch verifier's promise includes what it reads, what it may
write, which failures it must detect, when it must abstain, how uncertainty is
shown, what evidence it emits, how long its qualification lasts, who may rely
on it, and what happens when it is wrong. A replacement is governable only when
those obligations remain visible before, during, and after the swap.

## A Field Is a Promise, Not a Label

A conventional registry says which implementation currently answers a name.
A stable capability field says what must be true before any implementation may
answer that name.

For the patch verifier, the field might require that every decision identify
the repository revision, proposed diff, test plan, policy version, model and
tool versions, evidence consulted, unresolved uncertainty, and authority used.
It might require rejection when protected tests cannot run, abstention when the
change exceeds the verifier's competence, and human review when policy and
evidence conflict. It might forbid network access for confidential projects and
forbid the verifier from merging the patch it evaluates. It might preserve a
set of historical regressions that every successor must face.

These obligations define a capability only in context. The same verifier may
be qualified to advise a maintainer on a public documentation patch and
unqualified to approve a production authentication change. A model that is
adequate on one language, repository family, or threat model does not thereby
inherit every route bearing the same friendly name. Qualification is therefore
consumer-relative. It binds an exact consumer and use, not an imaginary global
score called capability.

The field also has a version. If the organization decides that the verifier may
now inspect secrets, approve database migrations, or replace human review for a
class of changes, the contract changed. Calling that an implementation upgrade
would hide a governance decision inside a technical release. A material change
to observables, authority, rights, effects, or recovery duties should produce a
new field version or a new field, with its own review.

This gives the system a disciplined answer to a deceptively simple question:
what stayed the same? It can point to the field version, required observables,
authority ceiling, preserved regressions, consumer scope, and recovery duties.
The answer may still be wrong; a record cannot guarantee semantic equivalence.
But it is specific enough to challenge, test, and revoke.

Without such a boundary, the system suffers capability amnesia. Release notes
remember that version two replaced version one, but the organization forgets
which old failure mattered, why a permission was denied, which evaluator was
trusted, or which downstream service relied on a particular abstention. The
new implementation appears to inherit the accumulated trust of the old one
while shedding the history that made that trust conditional.

Stable fields keep the memory with the capability. Incidents, regressions,
appeals, expired evidence, and prior limitations remain obligations of the
field rather than trivia attached to a retired artifact. An upgrade may resolve
them, but cannot make them disappear by changing implementation identity.

## Compatibility Is Not Qualification

Software engineering already offers useful tools for change: semantic
versioning, interface tests, provenance records, model registries, feature
flags, canary releases, rollout controllers, and rollback commands. The field
does not replace them. It explains why none is sufficient by itself.

An interface test can show that the new verifier accepts the same request
shape and emits the same response shape. It cannot show that `accept` still
means the same thing, that rare failures are preserved, or that a new remote
dependency did not widen the information boundary. Semantic versioning can
announce a breaking public change; it does not discover a behavioral change
the developer failed to name. Provenance can establish which source and build
produced an artifact; it cannot establish that the artifact is fit for this
field. A benchmark can compare selected outcomes; it does not own authority,
incident memory, state migration, or recovery.

Qualification asks a larger, scoped question. Does this exact candidate,
including its model, prompt, tools, data, dependencies, hardware, runtime, and
policy, preserve every required observable and authority obligation for this
consumer and use under this environment and threat model? Does it retain the
historical regressions? Can it migrate required state? Does it compose with
neighboring capabilities? Is the evaluator sufficiently independent of the
candidate and its training path? What happens when evidence is missing or has
expired?

The honest answers include *no* and *unknown*. Unknown is especially important.
Systems under delivery pressure often treat absence of a detected failure as a
pass. A stable field instead treats missing evidence as a route decision. The
candidate can remain in a sandbox, shadow role, or narrow canary while the
default stays unchanged. Progress is allowed without forcing uncertainty into
production.

Qualification is also an evidence lease rather than a permanent badge. It
names the exact implementation and dependencies, evaluator, workload,
environment, consumer, use, threat model, and evidence epoch. A dependency
change, new incident, evaluator update, provenance failure, policy revision,
hardware change, or expired monitoring window can narrow or revoke it. The
field does not say that the candidate became inherently safe. It says where
the available evidence currently permits routing.

For the patch verifier, the first lease might allow only public repositories
and low-risk changes, require human confirmation, and expire after thirty days
or after any policy update. The old verifier remains the default and fallback.
The candidate may earn a broader lease later, but it cannot borrow one from its
name.

## The Patch Verifier Replacement

Now return to the proposed upgrade. The team wants the new verifier because it
is faster and appears more accurate. A governed replacement begins before the
team observes the final comparison.

First, it freezes the transaction. The record names the field version, prior
implementation, candidate, dependency graph, repository population, allowed
change classes, authority ceiling, evaluator, historical regression set,
checkpoint, canary population, monitor, stop rules, commit rule, rollback
objective, residual owner, and review authority. Choosing these rules after
seeing the result would let the candidate select its own test.

Second, it classifies the change. The candidate uses a new model and retrieval
index, changes its prompt policy, adds a remote dependency, and alters how it
selects tests. Each delta is visible. The remote dependency may violate the
field for confidential repositories even if the model improves. A new output
meaning may require a field-version decision rather than an implementation
replacement. Classification prevents a large semantic change from entering
through a small deployment label.

Third, it freezes the pre-state and affected inventory. For this verifier, that
includes the route alias, model and prompt artifacts, policy bundle, retrieval
snapshot, test cache, credentials, monitor configuration, audit schema,
downstream approval rules, and any learned state produced from prior reviews.
The inventory also names surfaces it cannot restore, such as a decision already
shown to a maintainer or context already sent to an external service.

Fourth, the candidate runs in isolation. It may read selected repository
snapshots and produce recommendations, but it cannot merge, publish, change
credentials, update the default route, or train a descendant. Its decisions are
compared against historical cases, rare failures, adversarial patches, human
review, and the old verifier under matched conditions. Disagreements are
evidence to inspect, not inconveniences to average away.

Suppose the candidate performs well enough for a canary. The lease still names
which repositories and patch classes it may see, how much traffic it receives,
which decisions require human confirmation, how delayed outcomes will be
counted, and which monitor event immediately returns traffic to the prior
implementation. Silence is not success. Missing telemetry is itself a failure
condition because the canary cannot establish what no observer measured.

During the canary, the new verifier approves a change that reintroduces a
historical authentication defect. The ordinary performance metrics remain
healthy. Latency is lower. Most reviewers prefer the new explanations. The
regression-floor monitor nevertheless fails.

The transaction does not ask whether the candidate is promising overall. It
follows the preregistered branch. Default promotion is blocked. Canary traffic
returns to zero. The alias points back to the prior verifier. The candidate and
its evidence are quarantined for analysis. The failed attempt remains in the
field's history so the next candidate must face the same regression.

That outcome is not a wasted experiment. It discovered a boundary that the
average benchmark obscured and preserved it for future replacements. A system
that can learn from failed upgrades without normalizing them is more capable of
improvement than one that records only winners.

## Replacement Is a Transaction

The difference between installing an artifact and replacing a capability is
the difference between a file operation and a state transition with effects.

A real replacement can touch models, optimizer state, prompts, tools, policy,
data, caches, credentials, routes, monitors, user expectations, and downstream
systems. It may create external actions or disclosures. A canary can write
shared state or influence later training. A new schema can make the old system
unable to read the current state. A descendant may learn from outputs produced
while the candidate was active.

The transaction therefore has explicit stages: precheck, qualification,
canary, commit, monitor, rollback or compensation, quarantine, retirement, and
closure. These are not decorative labels. Each stage has an allowed authority,
required observations, failure route, and receipt. Passing precheck does not
authorize a canary. Starting a canary does not authorize default. Default does
not mean the monitor window is over. Restoring the old alias does not mean all
effects were reversed.

This staged model protects the old path while the new one proves itself. The
prior implementation remains identifiable and recoverable until closure. The
candidate cannot silently rewrite the qualification policy, its own evaluator,
or the evidence history. The monitor can trigger rollback even when product
pressure favors promotion. A failed branch terminates in an owned state rather
than falling between release tooling and incident response.

The transaction also distinguishes candidate quality from replacement
quality. A candidate can be better on the measured task while the replacement
is unacceptable because migration is lossy, authority widened, monitoring is
weak, rollback is incomplete, or operating cost overwhelms the benefit. A
candidate can be worse overall yet useful for a narrow route. The system should
make the routing decision from the joint contract rather than a single rank.

## Rollback Is Not Time Travel

Rollback is the most comforting word in an upgrade plan and one of the easiest
to misuse.

Pointing an alias back to the old verifier is a real recovery action. Restoring
the old model, prompt, policy, and cache can be real recovery too. But neither
reverses a secret sent to a remote service, a patch already merged, a user
decision made from the candidate's output, an audit record disclosed to an
outside party, or a descendant trained on the candidate's behavior. Some
effects can be replayed, some compensated, some contained, and some only
recorded as irreversible residuals.

The replacement transaction names a recovery objective before exposure. It
does not promise perfect reversal. It says which artifacts, state, services,
routes, credentials, policies, and downstream dependencies should match the
authorized checkpoint after rollback. It assigns owners for compensation,
notification, invalidation, disclosure response, or continuing containment
where equality is impossible.

This makes rollback testable. Reviewers can compare the declared pre-state with
the post-recovery state and say exactly which surfaces returned, which did not,
and why. A partial rollback may be the best available response. It becomes
misleading only when partial restoration is narrated as if the event never
happened.

The current technical work behind this chapter illustrates that boundary. One
bounded local campaign restored all twenty-four surfaces it had prospectively
declared across fifteen transactions, while finding no challenger with the
required utility gain. Another campaign achieved exact attack-control rollback
in thirty-two of thirty-six trials but produced only two useful releases,
below its gates. These are valuable negative results. They show that a declared
inventory can support exact local restoration and that strict governance can
still fail to produce useful replacement. They do not show complete semantic
or external-effect recovery, production rollback, or general safety.

The lesson is not that rollback is impossible. It is that recovery claims must
match their inventory. “The route alias and declared local state were restored”
is stronger engineering than “we rolled back everything” because the first can
be checked and the second usually cannot.

## Authority Must Not Ride Along

An implementation replacement is especially dangerous when capability and
authority are allowed to rise together.

Suppose the new verifier can call more tools than the old one. It can inspect a
private dependency service, trigger a deployment preview, or merge a trivial
change without human confirmation. Those features may be useful. They are not
evidence that the old field authorized them. The candidate must either remain
inside the existing ceiling or receive a separate governance grant attached to
a new field version or route.

This rule prevents a common form of capability laundering: a new component is
described as an implementation improvement, then gains broader effects because
its extra abilities are convenient. The field fixes authority independently of
implementation performance. A high score cannot grant a permission. A passing
test cannot appoint an evaluator. A canary cannot expand its own traffic. A
replacement record cannot promote its own evidence state.

Evaluator independence matters for the same reason. If the candidate wrote the
tests, selected the examples, influenced the monitor, and proposed the release,
then several nominally separate approvals may share one failure. Independence
is not a checkbox; it is a disclosed graph of models, data, prompts, tools,
people, organizations, and incentives. Where independence cannot be achieved,
the lease should narrow and the dependency should remain a residual.

## The Proof Boundary

Parts of this lifecycle are suitable for formal proof. A finite model can prove
that a mismatched field identity is rejected, that authority cannot expand
without a grant, that failed regression gates block promotion, that rejected
events leave the modeled state unchanged, that terminal quarantine absorbs
later suffixes, or that a monitor failure routes to rollback rather than
default.

These are useful results because transition logic is easy to get subtly wrong.
A system should not reach default through an invalid sequence. It should not
lose the prior implementation when a canary fails. It should preserve residual
ownership and refuse a record that omits a required rollback handle. Formal
models can make those structural promises exact over the records they define.

The proof ends at that boundary. It does not establish that the field captures
the real semantics of patch verification, that the regression suite is
competent, that the evaluator is actually independent, that the monitor sees
delayed harm, that an external service deleted the transmitted context, or that
restored files imply restored human trust. Those are empirical, institutional,
and semantic questions.

The architecture needs both kinds of work. Formal checks should prevent the
control record from contradicting itself. Real experiments and operations must
test whether the record corresponds to the world. Neither may borrow the
other's authority.

## Failure Cases

The first failure is **field drift**. The organization keeps the stable name
while gradually changing outputs, abstentions, permissions, users, and failure
meaning. Each individual change looks small. Taken together, they produce a
different capability that inherits the old one's trust. Version review must
therefore inspect cumulative semantic and authority change, not only the latest
diff.

The second is **qualification laundering**. A candidate passes an interface
test, provenance check, or benchmark and the narrow result is described as
qualification for the field. Each observation may be valid while the inference
is not. Qualification requires the conjunction named by the field for the
specific route; a strong score on one dimension cannot fill missing authority,
regression, migration, or recovery evidence.

The third is **evaluator capture**. The candidate and evaluator share a model,
training data, prompt author, retrieval system, organizational incentive, or
failure blind spot. Two agreeing outputs are then counted as independent
support. Dependency disclosure does not eliminate capture, but it can prevent
the system from assigning independence it did not earn and route the candidate
to a narrower lease.

The fourth is **canary leakage**. A supposedly isolated candidate writes to a
shared cache, updates a memory, influences a human decision, trains a
descendant, changes an external record, or exposes confidential context. Its
traffic share may be small while its effects are durable. Canary scope must
therefore cover reads, writes, learning, credentials, tools, network, external
effects, and descendant influence rather than only request percentage.

The fifth is **monitor blindness**. The rollout monitor sees latency and
immediate test outcomes but not delayed security defects, distributional harm,
appeals, downstream regressions, or changes in human reliance. A quiet monitor
window then becomes evidence of success. The transaction should name outcome
delay, missing-telemetry behavior, censoring, observation dependencies, and
post-commit review. Where the harm cannot be observed in time, exposure should
remain narrower.

The sixth is **checkpoint hindsight**. The team selects the prior or candidate
state after observing results, reports the best checkpoint rather than the
authorized final state, or changes the evaluation window to favor the upgrade.
Prospective checkpoint authority and a durable comparison history keep useful
exploration from becoming selective evidence.

The seventh is **rollback theater**. The old binary or alias is restored and
the incident closes even though data, caches, policies, credentials, services,
external actions, disclosures, descendants, or user reliance remain changed.
Recovery claims must enumerate the restored inventory and preserve every
unrestored effect as compensation work, containment, or an owned residual.

The eighth is **descendant escape**. A canary or short-lived default produces a
dataset, tool, policy, memory, or successor model that survives after the
candidate is rolled back. Restoring the parent route does not invalidate what
learned from it. The transaction needs descendant identity and invalidation
rules wherever replacement outputs can become durable causal inputs.

The ninth is **incident amnesia**. Retirement removes the old implementation
and its local documentation, taking historical failures with it. Future
candidates repeat the defect because the regression belonged to the artifact
rather than the field. The stable field should retain the incident and its
test, along with the limits of that test, after every implementation that
originally encountered it is gone.

The tenth is **governance overload**. Every low-risk replacement receives the
same elaborate packet, reviews slow to a halt, and operators begin copying
records without examining them. The machinery then adds ceremony while real
risk moves elsewhere. Field depth and transaction cost should scale with
authority, state, side effects, uncertainty, reversibility, and affected
consumers. Proportionality is not a waiver of governance; it is protection
against governance becoming uninformative.

These failures share one pattern: a true statement about one surface is allowed
to stand in for the whole replacement. The field and transaction are useful
only when they prevent that substitution. They should make narrow success
easier to state, broad success harder to counterfeit, and failure cheaper to
retain as knowledge.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest objection is not that change should be ungoverned. It is that
ordinary disciplined engineering may already be enough.

A competent team can use versioned interfaces, provenance, model registries,
feature flags, progressive delivery, canaries, regression suites, MLOps
pipelines, rollback rehearsal, incident response, and human approval. Adding a
stable-field object and a larger transaction may duplicate those practices,
slow useful upgrades, create new paperwork, and give a false impression that
semantic continuity has been certified.

This objection has force. The field should not survive merely because it can
describe more metadata. It must improve decisions that matter: detecting
semantic drift, preventing authority expansion, preserving rare regressions,
calibrating evidence expiry, exposing evaluator dependence, recovering more of
the declared state and effects, reducing repeated incidents, or making a failed
replacement easier to understand and contain. Those gains must be compared
against latency, compute, operator work, evaluator work, storage, missed help,
false blocking, and residual burden.

The architecture should also be allowed to shrink. A low-risk, stateless tool
with no privileged effects may need only a small field: interface, provenance,
tests, owner, expiry, and fallback. A high-risk verifier that influences release
authority needs more. Governance proportionality is part of the design. If the
same packet is required for every change, the system will either stop changing
or learn to fill forms without learning anything.

## From a Minimum Record to a Replacement Fabric

The minimum useful implementation is modest. Give one capability a stable ID
and versioned contract. Name its consumers, accepted inputs, required outputs,
abstentions, errors, side effects, authority ceiling, historical regressions,
candidate identity, evaluator, evidence lease, lifecycle state, fallback, and
rollback owner. Validate that missing identity, stale evidence, authority
widening, failed regressions, self-evaluation, absent fallback, or unowned
irreversible effects block the default route.

Then run one prospective replacement. Freeze the rules before results. Keep the
candidate isolated. Use a narrow canary with a real stop condition. Exercise
rollback before default. Compare the declared inventory after recovery. Keep
negative and null outcomes. This does not prove the architecture, but it turns
“upgrade” into a decision that can be inspected.

The mature system is a replacement fabric spanning models, tools, memory,
policies, data, evaluators, runtimes, and organizational procedures. Fields are
versioned and consumer-relative. Qualification evidence decays. Historical
incidents follow the field. Dependency changes trigger revalidation. Candidates
can remain shadowed or canaried without pressure to become default. Monitoring,
rollback, compensation, descendant invalidation, and retirement share one
lineage.

A serious research campaign would compare this fabric with registries,
interface-only checks, provenance-only admission, benchmark promotion,
progressive delivery, conventional MLOps, snapshot restoration, and the best
ordinary change-management baseline. It would use real stateful and
side-effecting capabilities, ambiguous boundaries, delayed outcomes,
irreversible effects, heterogeneous consumers, captured evaluators, and stale
evidence. It would measure useful improvement and blocked harm together.

The proposal should advance only if it is not dominated on that joint frontier.
If conventional methods preserve continuity and recovery at lower cost, the
field should narrow. If a mechanism adds paperwork without changing decisions,
remove it. If field boundaries prove too ambiguous for independent reviewers to
agree, do not disguise disagreement as a stable interface.

## The Strongest Objection

Stable names can hide exactly the semantic drift they are meant to expose.

Once a field becomes an important route, organizations may resist admitting
that its meaning changed. A committee can preserve the field ID, update a few
tests, and declare the candidate compatible. The stable abstraction then makes
incomparable systems look interchangeable. A rich record can worsen the problem
by giving the decision a technical appearance.

The answer cannot be more faith in the record. Field changes need dissent,
appeal, independent evaluation, incident memory, and a visible route to say
that the old and new implementations are not the same capability. Unknown and
incomparable must remain valid outcomes. A field version should split when
material obligations diverge, even when that complicates navigation or delays
an attractive release.

The objection also reaches rollback. An organization may declare success over
the surfaces it chose to inventory and ignore everything outside them. The
inventory must therefore be prospective, challengeable, and tied to affected
consumers and external effects. Omitted surfaces need reasons and owners. The
claim must stay inventory-specific.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

The architecture should be reduced if natural replacement studies show no
continuity, challenge, or recovery benefit beyond conventional versioning,
progressive delivery, and disciplined MLOps. It should change if independent
reviewers cannot agree on field boundaries, if evidence leases fail to predict
regression, if rollback inventories systematically omit consequential effects,
or if evaluator-separation records fail to reveal shared failure.

It should be rejected for a domain if the machinery blocks useful improvement
without reducing unsafe release, repeated incidents, authority drift, or
recovery burden. Positive evidence would need prospective comparisons across
real implementations, consumers, environments, update classes, and threat
models; complete denominators including failed and abandoned attempts;
independent evaluation; causal ablations of field identity, leases, regression
memory, authority ceilings, canary isolation, and recovery duties; and transfer
across organizations and substrates.

No finite proof, schema, fixture, or clean local rollback can answer that
question alone. The current technical work establishes bounded record and
transition behavior, plus narrow inventory-specific outcomes. The core claims
remain arguments awaiting broader evidence.

## What This Establishes

An improving system needs stable promises and replaceable machinery. Confusing
the two produces either stagnation or trust laundering.

Stable Capability Fields put identity, observable obligations, authority,
incident memory, evidence scope, and recovery duties above any one
implementation. Governed replacement turns an upgrade into a prospective,
staged transaction whose failures, partial reversals, and irreversible effects
remain visible. Together they make improvement contestable and reversible
where possible without pretending that a name, benchmark, or rollback command
proves equivalence.

The patch verifier may change. Its promise cannot change invisibly. The new
implementation earns only the route its evidence supports, for the consumers
and uses that were actually examined, during the period in which that evidence
remains current. When the canary fails, the system returns to the prior route,
keeps the failed result, and owns what could not be undone.

That is the handoff to the next problem. A replaceable capability can preserve
its contract and still reason from bad observations. Unit 10 begins the
cognitive path by asking what a system is entitled to believe about the world
it senses.
